text: Let $Pr(x)$: $x$ is prime, $G(x)$: $x > 2$, $O(x)$: $x$ is odd, over the positive integers. Which formula represents “every prime greater than 2 is odd”?
solution: The subject class is “primes greater than 2”: the filter is $Pr(x) \wedge G(x)$.
“Every A is B” pairs $\forall$ with $\to$: $\forall x((Pr(x) \wedge G(x)) \to O(x))$.
Check with a non-prime such as 4: the filter is false, the implication vacuously true, so 4 does not refute the sentence, as it should not.
concept: All A are B is ∀x(A(x) → B(x)); a two-condition subject becomes a conjunction inside the filter.

common_wrong.why: ∀ with ∧ claims every number is a prime greater than 2; 4 refutes it although the sentence is true.
∃ with → is true as soon as one number fails the filter (e.g. 1); it says almost nothing.
That is the converse, “every odd number is a prime greater than 2”, false at 9.

text: On the domain $\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5\}$ with the usual order, how many of these sentences are true? (i) $\forall x \exists y\,(x < y)$ (ii) $\exists y \forall x\,(x \le y)$ (iii) $\forall x \exists y\,(y < x \vee y = x)$ (iv) $\exists x \forall y\,(x \le y)$ (v) $\forall y \exists x\,(x < y)$
solution: (i) says there is no largest element: $x = 5$ is a counterexample. False.
(ii) some element is at least every element: $y = 5$. True. (iv) some element is at most every element: $x = 1$. True.
(iii) take $y = x$. True. (v) says there is no least element: $y = 1$ has nothing below it. False.
Three sentences are true.
concept: ∀x∃y lets the witness depend on x; ∃y∀x needs one witness for all. On a finite chain, 'no maximum' and 'no minimum' fail.

common_wrong.why: Reading (i) and (v) as true by forgetting that a finite domain has a largest and a smallest element.
Missing that $y = x$ is allowed in (iii); the disjunction makes it trivially true.

text: Which formula is equivalent to $\neg\forall x \exists y\,(P(x, y) \to Q(y))$?
solution: Flip each quantifier as the negation passes it: $\neg\forall x \exists y \equiv \exists x \forall y\,\neg$.
Negate the matrix: $\neg(P(x, y) \to Q(y)) \equiv P(x, y) \wedge \neg Q(y)$.
Result: $\exists x \forall y\,(P(x, y) \wedge \neg Q(y))$.
concept: Negation flips every quantifier it passes and negates the matrix; ¬(p → q) = p ∧ ¬q.

common_wrong.why: Negating an implication does not negate its conclusion only: ¬(p → q) is p ∧ ¬q, not p → ¬q.
The quantifiers were left unflipped; only the matrix was negated.
Both quantifiers became ∃ and the wrong parts were negated; ¬P ∧ Q is the negation of P ∨ ¬Q, not of P → Q.

text: Let $S(x)$: $x$ is a student and $F(x)$: $x$ failed. Which formulas represent “no student failed”?
solution: “No A is B” is $\neg\exists x(A \wedge B)$: option A.
Pushing the negation in gives $\forall x\,\neg(S \wedge F) \equiv \forall x(S \to \neg F)$: option B.
The contrapositive inside the quantifier, $S \to \neg F \equiv F \to \neg S$, gives option C (“nobody who failed is a student”).
Option D claims every object is a student; a world with one non-student refutes it while the sentence holds.
concept: No A is B: ¬∃x(A ∧ B) ≡ ∀x(A → ¬B) ≡ ∀x(B → ¬A).

common_wrong.why: C is the contrapositive of B inside the quantifier, so it is equivalent too.
D is the ∀-with-∧ trap: it makes everything a student.

text: Let $M(x)$: $x$ is a member and $V(x)$: $x$ can vote. Which formula represents “only members can vote”?
solution: “Only A are B” says being B requires being A: the necessary condition is the conclusion.
Here B = can vote, A = member: $\forall x(V(x) \to M(x))$.
It forbids exactly a non-member who votes, and says nothing about members who cannot vote.
concept: Only A are B = ∀x(B(x) → A(x)), the converse of 'all A are B'.

common_wrong.why: That is “all members can vote”, the converse; it allows non-members to vote.
That only says some voting member exists; it does not exclude non-members.
∀ with ∧ makes everything a voting member.

text: Let $D = \{a, b, c\}$. For how many of the $2^9$ binary relations $R$ on $D$ is $\exists y \forall x\, R(x, y)$ true?
solution: On the 3×3 grid (rows $x$, columns $y$) the sentence says some column is full.
A column is full in $1$ of its $2^3 = 8$ patterns, so it is not full in 7. The three columns are independent, so no column is full in $7^3 = 343$ relations.
Hence $512 - 343 = 169$ relations have a full column.
concept: ∃y∀x R(x, y): some column of the relation grid is full; count by the complement.

common_wrong.why: 343 counts the relations with **no** full column (and also, by coincidence, the relations where every row is non-empty, ∀x∃y R).
Counting the columns, not the relations.

text: With $L(x, y)$: $x$ loves $y$, which of these sentences is true in **every** interpretation?

options.t: $\exists y \forall x\, L(x, y) \to \forall x \exists y\, L(x, y)$
$\forall x \exists y\, L(x, y) \to \exists y \forall x\, L(x, y)$
$\forall x \exists y\, L(x, y) \to \exists x \forall y\, L(x, y)$
$\exists x \forall y\, L(x, y) \to \exists y \forall x\, L(x, y)$

solution: A: if one person $b$ is loved by everyone, then each $x$ loves someone (namely $b$). True in every interpretation (the order theorem).
B and C fail on a 3-cycle $a \to b \to c \to a$: everyone loves someone, but nobody is loved by all and nobody loves all.
D fails when $a$ loves everyone and nobody else loves anyone: $a$ loves all, but no one is loved by $b$.
concept: ∃y∀x ⇒ ∀x∃y is the only valid move across a ∃/∀ boundary.

common_wrong.why: That is the converse of the valid direction; the cycle is a counter-model.
“Someone loves everyone” is about a full row; “someone is loved by everyone” is about a full column. One row does not fill a column.

text: Which formulas say “exactly one element has property $P$”?

options.t: $\exists x\, P(x) \wedge \forall x \forall y\,((P(x) \wedge P(y)) \to x = y)$

solution: Test each on three worlds: $P$ empty, $P$ with one element, $P$ with two elements. A correct formula gives F, T, F.
A (existence + every other $P$ is the same): F, T, F. B (the $P$'s are exactly $x$): F, T, F. C (at least one and at most one): F, T, F.
D says “at least two”: F, F, T.
concept: Exactly one = existence + uniqueness; three standard equivalent forms.

common_wrong.why: B is the compact form: $P(y) \leftrightarrow y = x$ says the $P$'s are precisely $x$.
D is “at least two”, the negation of “at most one”.

text: Which variables occur free in $\forall x\,(P(x) \to \exists y\, R(x, y, z)) \wedge Q(x)$?
solution: The bracket after $\forall x$ closes before $\wedge\, Q(x)$, so the $x$ in $Q(x)$ is outside every quantifier on $x$: free.
$y$ is bound by $\exists y$; $z$ has no quantifier: free.
Free variables: $x$ (in $Q(x)$) and $z$.
concept: A variable is free where it lies outside the scope of every quantifier on it; a letter can be bound in one place and free in another.

common_wrong.why: The $x$ in $Q(x)$ lies outside the bracket that $\forall x$ governs.
$y$ appears only inside $\exists y$, so it is bound.
$z$ is never quantified.

text: On the domain $\{1, 2, \dots, 10\}$, for how many $x$ is $\forall y\,((y \mid x \wedge y > 1) \to Even(y))$ true?
solution: The formula says every divisor of $x$ greater than 1 is even, i.e. $x$ has no odd divisor above 1: $x$ is a power of 2.
Powers of 2 in range: 2, 4, 8.
And $x = 1$: it has no divisor greater than 1, so every implication is vacuously true. Total $4$ (1, 2, 4, 8).
concept: A restricted ∀ over an empty restriction is vacuously true.

common_wrong.why: Forgetting $x = 1$, where the filter is empty and the ∀ holds vacuously.
Counting the even numbers; 6 and 10 have the odd divisors 3 and 5.

text: Which one of the following formulas is **valid** (domains are non-empty)?

options.t: $\forall x\,(P(x) \vee Q(x)) \to (\forall x\, P(x) \vee \forall x\, Q(x))$
$(\exists x\, P(x) \wedge \exists x\, Q(x)) \to \exists x\,(P(x) \wedge Q(x))$

solution: $\forall x(P \wedge Q)$ gives $\forall x\, P$ (law 2), and $\forall x\, P \Rightarrow \exists x\, P$ on a non-empty domain: pick any element.
(A) and (B) are the converses of the one-way laws; the world $D = \{0, 1\}$, $P = \{0\}$, $Q = \{1\}$ makes each hypothesis true and each conclusion false.
concept: ∀ distributes over ∧, and ∀ ⇒ ∃ needs only a non-empty domain; ∀ over ∨ and ∃ over ∧ go one way only.

common_wrong.why: That is ∀ distributed over ∨, valid only from right to left.
Two separate witnesses need not be the same element.
One element with $P$ does not make every element a $P$.

text: Consider all interpretations of the unary predicates $P$ and $Q$ on the domain $\{0, 1\}$ (there are 16). In how many of them is $\forall x\,(P(x) \vee Q(x)) \to (\forall x\, P(x) \vee \forall x\, Q(x))$ **false**?
solution: The implication is false exactly when every element has $P$ or $Q$, but $P$ is not universal and $Q$ is not universal.
Some element lacks $P$; it must then have $Q$. Some element lacks $Q$; it must then have $P$. These are different elements, so one element is $P$-only and the other $Q$-only.
That gives $P = \{0\}, Q = \{1\}$ or $P = \{1\}, Q = \{0\}$: **2** interpretations.
concept: Counter-models of ∀ over ∨ are exactly the 'split' worlds.

common_wrong.why: Counting worlds where $P$ and $Q$ are both non-universal without requiring $\forall x(P \vee Q)$.
The formula is not valid; only its converse is.

$\neg(P \to Q) \equiv P \wedge \neg Q$.
Result: $\forall x \exists y\,(P(x, y) \wedge \neg Q(y))$.
concept: Each quantifier flips as the ¬ passes it; a negated implication is 'hypothesis and not conclusion'.

common_wrong.why: Negated the wrong side of the implication.
Forgot to flip the quantifiers.
Pushed the ¬ only into the conclusion and kept both quantifiers.

text: $W$ is a formula with no free occurrence of $x$. Which of the following are valid?
solution:
(A) $ orall x(
eg P \vee W) \equiv  orall x\,
eg P \vee W \equiv 
eg\exists x P \vee W$: the quantifier flips out of the hypothesis. Valid.
(B) $W$ is the hypothesis, $P(x)$ the conclusion: no flip. Valid (non-empty domain).
(C) keeps ∀ in the hypothesis position: false with $D = \{0, 1\}$, $P = \{0\}$, $W$ = F.
(D) ∃ over ∨ and null quantification: valid.
concept: A quantifier leaving the hypothesis of → flips; everywhere else it stays.

common_wrong.why: (C) is the classic unflipped version; it fails when $P$ holds somewhere but not everywhere and $W$ is false.
(A) is right: the ∀ must become ∃ when it leaves the hypothesis.

text: Which sentence is **implied** by $\exists y \forall x\, R(x, y)$?
solution: A witness $b$ with $R(a, b)$ for every $a$ serves as the $y$ for each $x$: $\forall x \exists y R$ follows.
In the grid (rows $x$, columns $y$) the hypothesis is 'a full column'. The world $R = \{(0, 0), (1, 0)\}$ has a full column 0 but no full row (C), not all pairs (A), and column 1 empty (D).
concept: ∃y∀x ⇒ ∀x∃y: a full column puts a 1 in every row.

common_wrong.why: One full column is not the whole grid.
A full column is not a full row.
'Every column has a 1' is about columns; one column can be full while another is empty.

text: What is the smallest size of a domain on which $\forall x \exists y\, R(x, y) \wedge \forall x \forall y\,(R(x, y) \to \neg R(y, x))$ has a model?
solution: Asymmetry with $y = x$ forbids loops, so each element needs a successor different from itself.
Two elements: $0 \to 1$ and $1 \to 0$ are forced, which breaks asymmetry. So size 2 is impossible.
Three elements: the cycle $0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 0$ works. Answer **3**.
concept: Without transitivity a serial asymmetric relation can close into a cycle of length 3; with transitivity it cannot be finite.

common_wrong.why: On two elements the forced pairs $(0,1), (1,0)$ violate asymmetry.
A single element would need $R(0,0)$, a loop, which asymmetry forbids.

text: Which first-order sentence is equivalent to the logic-program rule $P(x) \leftarrow Q(x, y), R(y)$?
solution: The rule is $\forall x \forall y\,(Q(x, y) \wedge R(y) \to P(x))$.
$y$ occurs only in the body, so $\forall y$ moves into the hypothesis as $\exists y$.
concept: Body-only variables of a Horn rule are existential inside the hypothesis.

common_wrong.why: ∀y inside the hypothesis demands every y, far too weak.
That reverses the arrow (head → body).
∃y outside asks for one y that works for the rule; the rule must hold for every y.

text: A prenex form of $\forall x\, P(x) \vee \forall x\, Q(x)$ is
solution: Rename the second bound variable: $\forall x\, P(x) \vee \forall y\, Q(y)$.
Pull $\forall x$ and then $\forall y$ out (each part lacks the other variable).
concept: Rename bound variables apart before pulling; ∀ does not merge over ∨.

common_wrong.why: Merging the two ∀ is the one-way law (a) run backwards.
∃y gives $\forall x P(x) \vee \exists y Q(y)$.
∃x gives $\exists x P(x) \vee \forall y Q(y)$.

text: Which of the following sentences have **no finite model** (but at least one infinite model)?

options.t: $\forall x \exists y\, R(x, y) \wedge \forall x\, \neg R(x, x) \wedge \forall x \forall y \forall z\,(R(x, y) \wedge R(y, z) \to R(x, z))$
$\forall x \exists y\, R(x, y) \wedge \forall x\, \neg R(x, x)$
$\forall x \exists y\, R(x, y) \wedge \forall x \forall y\,(R(x, y) \to \neg R(y, x))$
$\exists x \forall y\, \neg R(y, x) \wedge \forall x \exists y\, R(x, y) \wedge \forall x\, \neg R(x, x) \wedge \forall x \forall y \forall z\,(R(x, y) \wedge R(y, z) \to R(x, z))$

solution: (A): irreflexive + transitive implies asymmetric ($R(x,y), R(y,x)$ would give $R(x,x)$). So (A) is the 1991 sentence: $(\mathbb{N}, <)$ is a model, no finite model.
(D) adds 'some element has no predecessor' to (A); $(\mathbb{N}, <)$ with $x = 0$ still works, and finite models are still impossible.
(B): $R = \{(0, 1), (1, 0)\}$ is a two-element model. (C): the 3-cycle is a model.
concept: A serial strict order forces an infinite chain; drop transitivity (or asymmetry) and a finite cycle appears.

common_wrong.why: (D) only adds a condition that $(\mathbb{N}, <)$ meets; it still has no finite model.
(B) has the two-element model $0 \leftrightarrow 1$: nothing forbids a 2-cycle without transitivity.

text: Every satisfiable sentence of the form $\exists a \exists b \exists c \exists d\, \forall u \forall v\, \psi$ ($\psi$ quantifier-free, predicates and equality only, no function symbols) has a model with at most $m$ elements. What is the least such $m$?
solution: By the small-model theorem, restricting any model to the 4 witnesses gives a model of size at most 4.
4 is needed: with $\psi$ = '$a, b, c, d$ are pairwise different', every model has at least 4 elements.
concept: An ∃^k∀* sentence without functions has a model of size ≤ k, and k can be forced.

common_wrong.why: The number of universal variables does not bound the model; the existentials do.
Only the existential witnesses must be kept.

text: Over the natural numbers, which statement is TRUE for **every** predicate $P$?
solution: Steps of 2 need two bases: induct on $S(k) = P(2k) \wedge P(2k + 1)$.
(A) fails for 'x is even'; (C) fails for 'x ≥ 1' (0 is missed); (D) steps downwards and fails for 'x = 0'.
concept: A step of size d needs d consecutive bases starting at 0, and the step must point upwards.

common_wrong.why: From 0 with steps of 2 you reach only the even numbers.
Base 1 never reaches 0.
$P(x+1) \to P(x)$ moves towards 0, never upwards.

text: The sentence $\forall x \forall y\,(R(x, y) \to R(y, x)) \wedge \exists x \exists y\, R(x, y) \wedge \forall x\, \neg R(x, x)$ is

options.t: satisfiable, and so is its negation
satisfiable, but only in infinite domains

solution: Model: $D = \{0, 1\}$, $R = \{(0, 1), (1, 0)\}$ (symmetric, a pair, no loops).
Counter-model: $D = \{0\}$, $R = \varnothing$ (no pair at all). So both the sentence and its negation are satisfiable.
concept: To classify a sentence, exhibit one model and one counter-model.

common_wrong.why: With $R$ empty the middle conjunct fails.
The two-element symmetric pair is a model.
A two-element model exists.

text: On the domain $\{0, 1, 2\}$, in how many of the 8 interpretations of the unary predicate $P$ is $\exists x\,(P(x) \to \forall y\, P(y))$ **false**?
solution: $\forall y P(y)$ has no free $x$, so $\exists x(P(x) \to W) \equiv \forall x P(x) \to W$ with $W = \forall y P(y)$.
That is $X \to X$: true in every interpretation. Answer **0**.
concept: Null quantification flips ∃ to ∀ out of a hypothesis; the 'trigger' sentence is valid.

common_wrong.why: The world where every element has P makes the sentence true (any x works).
If some element lacks P, choose it as x: the implication is vacuously true.
